## Key Takeaways


- Procurement innovation enhances delivery models to meet complex infrastructure demands faster.
- Owner’s Advisory provides a program-level view, helping decision-makers align requirements with execution.
- Faster acquisition, through approaches like OTAs, necessitates stricter delivery discipline and integrated management.
- Case studies like the METC illustrate the importance of owner-side perspectives in managing complex projects effectively.
- Overall success in federal infrastructure relies on coordinated action rather than just meeting individual project requirements.


### **Procurement innovation is most powerful when the delivery model is equipped to keep pace**


Federal agencies are being asked to deliver critical infrastructure faster, even as the environments they’re building become more complex. But speed alone does not produce mission-ready outcomes. As programs become more complex, the greater challenge isto strengthen the owner’s ability to make the right decisions as the program moves faster.


Mission-critical infrastructure is more than a collection of facilities. Physical assets, secure systems, technology, utilities, construction, and operational requirements must work together in support of a common mission. The greatest risks often emerge where those elements meet across contracts, disciplines, and phases of delivery.


That’s where an integrated owner-side perspective can make a difference.


The Owner’s Advisor gives government leaders a program-level view, connecting requirements, governance, acquisition, cost, schedule, construction, commissioning, and operational readiness to the decisions the owner must make. The aim isn’t to add another layer of management. It’s helping the owner maintain authority and visibility across an increasingly complex delivery environment.


### Better Decisions Create Speed


There is a tendency to think of faster delivery as a scheduling problem: shorten the phases, accelerate procurement, and start construction sooner. But some of the most valuable time on a complex program should be spent before construction begins.


Requirements shape design. Design choices influence procurement and construction sequencing, which impacts systems integration, commissioning, and turnover. Physical completion alone doesn’t make an asset mission-ready.


That means speed is partly a function of when decisions are made and how well their downstream impacts are understood.


We’ve applied the same principle across other complex programs. Integrated delivery creates value by giving owners visibility into decisions and dependencies while they still have options, rather than waiting for conflicts to emerge downstream.


Owner’s Advisory applies that principle from the customer’s side of the table. By connecting requirements and decision rights with cost, schedule, risk, design, construction, and readiness, we can help owners act earlier and keep execution aligned with the mission.


### USSPACECOM: Owner’s Advisory At Mission Scale


Our work on the new[U.S. Space Command headquarters at Redstone Arsenal](https://www.parsons.com/2026/09/parsons-awarded-85m-agreement-to-deliver-new-u-s-space-command-headquarters/) provides a tangible example. Under an Other Transaction Authority (OTA) agreement, we’re serving as Owner’s Advisor for development of the new headquarters, providing program and construction management support across scope, cost, schedule, quality, and risk, throughout every phase of the project lifecycle.


The most important element in this approach is the continuity it creates across the program.


When the same owner-side perspective extends from planning through operations, decisions can be evaluated against what the mission ultimately requires to make the best overall decisions for the program lifecycle.


### Faster Acquisition Raises The Stakes


The acquisition environment adds another dimension.


Alternative acquisition approaches, such as OTAs, can create new pathways for federal programs. Federal agencies are increasingly using OTAs to accelerate critical capabilities, streamline procurement, and access innovative solutions beyond traditional acquisition pathways. But a faster acquisition pathway doesn’t reduce the need for delivery discipline. It increases it.


Requirements still must be translated into executable decisions. Cost, schedule, quality, and risk still need to be managed. Design still has consequences for construction and operations. Commissioning and turnover still determine whether completed infrastructure can perform as intended.


As acquisition accelerates, there’s less room for disconnected decisions to surface later as program problems.


That is why we see alternative acquisition and Owner’s Advisory as complementary rather than separate innovations. One can change how a government customer moves toward execution. The other can help maintain continuity and control as that execution advances.


The real objective isn’t simply faster acquisition. It’s faster progress toward mission readiness. Our experience with OTAs spans infrastructure and mission technology, reinforcing a broader lesson: procurement innovation is most powerful when the delivery model is equipped to capitalize on it.


### METC: Where Speed And Complexity Converge


The Medical Education and Training Campus (METC) at Joint Base San Antonio–Fort Sam Houston brings that challenge into focus.


As a joint-service training hub, METC prepares enlisted personnel from across the services for medical roles and plays an important role in building the medical capabilities the Joint Force depends on.


The need for new housing became urgent in summer 2026, when approximately 5,200 students were relocated after serious problems were identified in the existing dormitories, including climate-control and foundation issues that could not be addressed through routine repairs. Five replacement buildings are designed to house up to 6,000 students.


Replacing that housing is therefore about more than recapitalizing facilities. It’s about providing safe, functional living environments for service members as they prepare for critical medical roles.


### **Accelerating Delivery at Scale**


Under an OTA agreement, the project will deliver five dormitories of approximately 400,000 square feet each, along with two central utility plants and related infrastructure. The use of off-site manufacturing is intended to accelerate the previously planned timeline by approximately 70 percent, targeting completion within 24 months, while reducing overall project costs by an anticipated 20 percent.


Volumetric modular construction (VMC) is central to that strategy. Building components are manufactured off site as three-dimensional modules and transported to the site for assembly, with modules expected to arrive roughly 95 percent complete.


Shifting that much activity into a factory environment can change more than where construction takes place. It makes early decisions about design, interfaces, quality assurance, transportation, logistics, utilities, and site construction increasingly consequential.


The faster the delivery model moves, the more important those connections become.


### **Maintaining The Owner’s View**


That’s where Owner’s Advisory will add value. Across the dormitories, modular assembly, central utility plants, construction activities, infrastructure, and eventual turnover, individual elements have to contribute to the performance of the program as a whole. Our role is to help the owner maintain visibility across those interfaces as the program advances.


Our Owner’s Advisory scope includes program governance, progressive design oversight, and construction management for the new dormitory facilities, central utility plant, and related infrastructure. The work also builds on our previous support to a $3.2 billion Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) and Military Construction (MILCON) program encompassing more than 180 projects across facilities, utilities, and infrastructure at Joint Base San Antonio.


The scale and pace of that integration make METC a tangible example of why increasingly accelerated programs need an equally integrated owner-side perspective. The value of that work can extend beyond METC. By capturing lessons learned throughout the program, we’re developing a repeatable Owner’s Advisor Program Management Guide for consideration on future Air Force Civil Engineer Center (AFCEC) programs.


### The Next Edge In Federal Infrastructure


Programs like METC point to a broader opportunity in federal infrastructure delivery. Success shouldn’t be measured only by whether individual projects meet their requirements, but by whether the program as a whole


That’s the value of Owner’s Advisory: bringing the right perspectives together early enough to influence the outcome and helping owners turn complexity into coordinated action.


It’s a shift from managing projects to shaping outcomes.
